# Spot the mood behind customer reviews with Hugging Face's free sentiment tool

> **In short:** Hugging Face runs a free web tool that reads any short text — including customer reviews — and labels it Positive or Negative with a confidence score. Paste your reviews in one at a time (or a few at once) and you can sort customer feedback by mood without rereading every word yourself.

Customer reviews pile up faster than any small team can read them. The good news: Hugging Face — a popular AI platform — offers a free sentiment analysis tool on its website that does the first pass for you. You paste a review, the tool tells you whether it leans positive or negative, and how confident it is. This guide walks you through it step by step, using only your browser.

## Before you start
- **A free Hugging Face account** — sign up at huggingface.co with an email address. No credit card needed.
- **A computer with a web browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari all work). The tool also loads on a phone, but a computer is easier for copy-paste.
- **Roughly 10 reviews copied into a plain text file** — short ones (one or two sentences each) work best. You can grab them from anywhere: Google reviews, Amazon, app store feedback, your own survey responses.
- **About 10 minutes total.** Most of that time is copying and pasting.
- **Honest expectation:** this is a first-pass filter, not a research-grade analysis. It sometimes misreads sarcasm, very short comments ("ok"), or reviews that mix positive and negative feelings in one sentence. Plan to glance at the results, not to trust them blindly.

## Step 1 — Open the sentiment tool in your browser

In your browser's address bar, type `huggingface.co` and press Enter. Once the site loads, look for the search bar at the very top (it usually says "Search models, datasets, users…" inside it). Click inside that bar and type **sentiment analysis**, then press Enter. A list of tools appears — the first one is usually called **"distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"** with a friendly label like *"Text Classification"* and a small green play icon. Click on that result.

**What you'll see:** a page with the model's name, a short description, and on the right-hand side a small box labeled **"Hosted inference API"** or **"Inference Widget"**. Inside that box there's a text area with the placeholder *"Type something…"* or *"Input text here."*

**What happens after:** the page is ready to accept your text. You don't need to read the rest of the page — just stay focused on that right-hand box.

**If it looks different:** Hugging Face redesigns its site from time to time. If you don't see a search bar, look for a **magnifying glass icon** 🔍 at the top of the page. If the result page doesn't show an input box, scroll down slowly — the input box is sometimes lower on the page, not on the right.

**You'll know it worked when** you can see a text box you can click into and type, with a small button underneath labeled something like **"Compute"** or **"Run"**.

💬 Example: you don't type anything yet in this step — just get to the page.

## Step 2 — Sign in so the tool will accept longer text

Click the **"Compute"** button once without typing anything. A small message will pop up saying something like *"You must be logged in to use this widget"* or *"Authentication required."* That's normal. Click **"Login"** or **"Sign in"** at the top-right corner of the page. Enter your email and password, or create a free account if you haven't yet (it takes about a minute: email, password, and a confirmation click).

**What you'll see:** after signing in, the page reloads and your profile picture (or initials) appears in the top-right corner instead of the "Login" button.

**What happens next:** the tool is now ready to accept real text from your account.

**If it looks different:** some browsers stay logged in after the first visit, so you might not see the pop-up at all. That's fine — just move on to Step 3.

**You'll know it worked when** your name or avatar shows in the top-right corner of the page.

💬 Example: not applicable in this step.

## Step 3 — Paste your first review and run the tool

Go to your text file of reviews and copy the first one — just one or two sentences. Click into the text box on the right side of the Hugging Face page and paste the review there. Then click the **"Compute"** button underneath the box.

**What you'll see:** a short wait (usually 1–3 seconds), then a small result panel appears. It shows a label — usually **"POSITIVE"** or **"NEGATIVE"** in capital letters — followed by a percentage like **"98.67%"**. That percentage is the model's confidence: how sure it is about its answer.

**What happens next:** the original review stays in the box, and the result sits right below it. You can now copy the result somewhere, or just leave it on screen and run the next one.

**If it looks different:** some reviews return two labels instead of one — for example **"POSITIVE: 97%"** and **"NEGATIVE: 3%"**. That's normal; it means the model is very sure the review is positive. Just read the bigger number.

**You'll know it worked when** you see a percentage above 50% next to either POSITIVE or NEGATIVE. Anything below 60% confidence is a "soft" result — the model isn't very sure, so read that review yourself.

💬 Example: paste this real-looking review to test: *"I've been using this coffee maker for three months and it still works perfectly. Worth every penny."* Expected result: POSITIVE, around 95% or higher.

## Step 4 — Paste a few reviews at once to save time

Here's the time-saver: you can paste multiple reviews into the same text box at once, separated by a blank line. The tool will return one result per paragraph. Click into the box, delete the first review, and paste two or three new ones, leaving a full empty line between each.

**What you'll see:** after you click **"Compute"**, the result panel shows several labels stacked vertically — one for each paragraph you pasted. Each one has its own POSITIVE or NEGATIVE label with a percentage.

**What happens next:** you can now scroll through the list and quickly spot which reviews came back negative — those are usually the ones worth reading first. Reviews above 90% negative confidence are the most likely complaints.

**If it looks different:** if the tool only returns one result when you pasted three reviews, the paragraphs probably weren't separated by a truly empty line. Press **Enter** twice (so there's a blank line between each review) and try again.

**You'll know it worked when** the number of labels in the result panel matches the number of reviews you pasted.

💬 Example: paste these three reviews, separated by blank lines: *"Shipping was fast and the product is solid."* / *"Total waste of money. Broke after a week."* / *"It's fine, does what it says."* Expected results: POSITIVE (~95%), NEGATIVE (~98%), and either one — but the middle one will clearly stand out as the complaint.

## Step 5 — Copy your results into a simple spreadsheet

This is where the time savings show up. Open a free tool — Google Sheets, Excel, or even a plain Notepad file works. For each review, type or paste the review text in one column and the model's result (POSITIVE or NEGATIVE plus the percentage) in the next column.

**What you'll see:** a growing table that looks like a spreadsheet. As you go, you'll start to see patterns — most reviews positive, a clear cluster of negatives, maybe a few mixed-feeling ones with low confidence.

**What happens next:** when you're done, you can **sort** the spreadsheet by the result column. In Google Sheets, click the column header, then choose **Data → Sort range**. The negative reviews jump to the top automatically. That's your shortlist for follow-up.

**If it looks different:** if you don't want to use a spreadsheet, even a simple text file works. Just write the review and the label next to it, like *"Broken after a week — NEGATIVE 99%."*

**You'll know it worked when** you can sort or scan your list and instantly see which reviews need a human response.

💬 Example: row format — Review: "Customer service was unhelpful and rude." | Sentiment: NEGATIVE 96% | Action: follow up personally.

## Step 6 — Spot the soft results and re-read them yourself

Scroll through your spreadsheet and look for any result where the confidence is **below 80%**. Those are the ones the model wasn't sure about. Open each of those reviews and read them yourself — they often contain sarcasm ("Oh sure, *great* service"), mixed feelings ("Shipping was great but the product is awful"), or very short comments ("meh", "10/10 would not recommend") that confuse simple models.

**What you'll see:** maybe 10–20% of your reviews fall into this "unsure" zone. That's expected.

**What happens next:** you decide what to do with each one — treat it as positive, negative, or neutral based on your own judgment. The tool saved you from re-reading the easy 80%; you only need to focus on the tricky ones.

**If it looks different:** if nearly every result comes back with low confidence (below 60%), the reviews may be in a language other than English, or they may be very technical. The English-only model struggles with both. In that case, the tool isn't useful for this batch — try a different sample.

**You'll know it worked when** you have a clean, sorted list of reviews where the obvious complaints are flagged and only the ambiguous handful needs human eyes.

💬 Example: a soft result to watch for — *"Wow, just what I always wanted… another thing that doesn't work."* The model might score this as POSITIVE because of the words "wanted" and "works," missing the sarcasm. You'll catch that on re-read.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting a wall of text instead of separate reviews.** The tool returns one result per paragraph, so an unbroken blob gives you one unhelpful score. Always press **Enter** twice between reviews.
- **Trusting a 55% confidence result.** Anything below 80% is the model shrugging. Treat those as "unsure" and read them yourself.
- **Using reviews in another language.** This particular model is English-only. Spanish, French, or Hungarian reviews will return random or low-confidence scores. For multilingual reviews, look for a model labeled **"multilingual"** in the search results instead.
- **Expecting it to catch sarcasm.** It usually doesn't. A sarcastic "best purchase ever 🙄" may be tagged POSITIVE because of the word "best." Always skim the negative-confidence results that contain words like "best," "love," "amazing" — the sarcasm lives there.
- **Forgetting to log in.** Without an account, the widget may refuse to run, or it may give you just one free try before asking you to sign up.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** if you run a small Etsy shop, a side-business on Amazon, or a local service with a Google profile, this tool lets you triage new reviews in the time it takes to drink a coffee. Negative reviews with high confidence go to the top of your reply list.
- **For your business or work:** if you handle customer feedback as part of your job — support, product, marketing — you can use this as a first-pass filter before sending feedback to a team. Even a rough "70% negative / 30% positive" split across 200 reviews is useful for spotting trends. For deeper analysis (themes, keywords, summary), you'd need a paid tool, but for a daily sanity check, this is free and fast.
- **If you're just getting started:** pick your five most recent reviews, paste them in one by one, and see what comes back. That's the fastest way to feel how the tool behaves before you commit to a bigger batch.

## Try it now
Open a new browser tab, go to huggingface.co, search for "sentiment analysis," click the first result, and paste this single review to test the tool end-to-end: *"Honestly, this was the worst customer experience I've had in years. Nothing worked and nobody replied to my emails."* Click **Compute**. You should see NEGATIVE with a confidence above 95%. That one test takes less than two minutes — and once it works, you know the rest of the guide will too.
